title: Finding things: globs and find
summary: Let the shell expand patterns, and let find search the tree.

steps.title: Globs: the shell expands, not the command
body: When you type `ls *.log`, **bash** replaces `*.log` with the matching names *before* `ls` runs. `ls` just sees `ls app.log error.log`.
| `*` | any run of characters (not a leading `.`, not `/`) |
| `{a,b}` | *brace expansion*: generates `a` and `b`, whether or not they exist |
notes.txt *.md          # no .md file: the pattern stays as-is

steps.prompt: The directory holds `a1.txt a2.txt b1.txt ab.txt c10.txt`. What does `echo [ab]?.txt` print?
steps.explain: `[ab]` is one character from {a, b}, `?` is exactly one more character. `c10.txt` fails the first, and the shell sorts matches alphabetically.

steps.prompt: You run `rm * .bak` (note the space). What happens?
options: Every file in the directory is deleted, then rm complains `.bak` doesn't exist
steps.explain: The space makes two arguments: `*` (everything) and `.bak`. Run `echo rm * .bak` first to see what the shell will actually pass.

steps.title: find: search the tree
body: Globs only look in one directory. `find` walks a whole tree and tests each entry.
find /var/log -name "*.gz"              # by name (quote the glob so find gets it, not bash)
find /tmp -mtime +7                     # modified more than 7 days ago
find . -name "*.log" -exec gzip {} \;   # run a command per match
`locate` is faster (it reads a prebuilt index) but can be stale. `which dotnet` tells you which program a command name runs.

steps.prompt: Find regular **files** under `/srv` ending in `.log` and older than 30 days, then delete them.
steps.explain: Tests are ANDed left to right. Put `-delete` last: find evaluates in order, and `-delete` first would delete everything.

steps.prompt: Match the need to the tool.
pairs: Quickly locate a file anywhere by name

steps.prompt: Arrange a safe workflow for bulk-deleting old temp files.
steps.explain: Look at what matches, count it, then act. The same expression each time, with the destructive action added last.

steps.title: Globs, find and xargs -0 on a messy drive
prompt: `~/shared` is a team drive that grew for years. Tidy it with the real tools:
1. Move the **first-quarter** reports (`report-2031-01-*.csv` to `report-2031-03-*.csv`, not the `.bak`) into
2. Delete the `.tmp` files in `~/shared/tmp` that are **older than 30 days**. Keep the newer ones and anything that is not `.tmp`.
3. Some names have spaces. Write into `~/answers/todo.txt` the path of every file under `~/shared` that contains
`TODO`, one per line. Use `find ... -print0 | xargs -0 grep -l` (or `grep -rl`).

checks.name: the six Q1 reports are in q1/
checks.fail: `~/shared/reports/q1/` should hold exactly the six January to March `.csv` reports. A bracket glob like `report-2031-0[1-3]-*.csv` matches them.

checks.name: the other reports stayed where they were
checks.fail: The `.bak` file, the summary and the April to June reports should still be in `~/shared/reports`. Your glob matched too much: press Reset scenario and try again.

checks.name: old .tmp files are gone
checks.fail: There are still `.tmp` files older than 30 days. `find ~/shared/tmp -name '*.tmp' -mtime +30` lists them; add `-delete` once the list looks right.

checks.name: new .tmp files and other files are kept
checks.fail: The recent `session-*.tmp` files or `old-but-keep.log` were deleted too. Only `.tmp` files older than 30 days should go.

checks.name: todo.txt lists every file with a TODO
checks.fail: `~/answers/todo.txt` should list the four files that contain `TODO`, including the ones with spaces in their names.

hints: Check a glob before you use it: `echo ~/shared/reports/report-2031-0[1-3]-*.csv` shows what the shell will pass to `mv`.
For age: `find ~/shared/tmp -name '*.tmp' -mtime +30` (more than 30 whole days). Run it without `-delete` first.
`find ~/shared -type f -print0 | xargs -0 grep -l TODO > ~/answers/todo.txt`: `-print0` and `-0` separate names with a NUL byte, so spaces cannot split them.
explain: The shell expands a glob **before** `mv` runs, so `echo` with the same glob is a free dry run. `find` is the tool when
the rule is about age, size or depth. Without `-print0`/`-0`, `xargs` splits `plan q2.md` into two words and grep
fails on files that do not exist: the classic bug in cleanup scripts.

steps.title: Mission: the lost report
prompt: On a shared drive with 300 files, `find` and `grep -r` earn their keep. In the mission **The lost report**, solve **Find the Biscuit Index**: nobody remembers the file name, only a line inside it.
steps.explain: `find` searches by what a file *is* (name, size, age, type); `grep -r` by what it *contains*. Combining them is the everyday way to find anything.
